message: Our basketball team won 45% of its games last season under the old head coach (37 of 82). Twenty games into this season under the new coach, we've won 11 and lost 9, which is 55%. The general manager is telling the press that the new coach is clearly better than the old one, and I agree; ten points is a big jump. The schedule so far has included some weaker opponents, but it's hard to say how much weaker on balance. Several players have also changed since last season. Can we go with "the new coach is better" in our season preview?
response:
No, I wouldn't print "the new coach is better." The record so far doesn't support it, statistically or otherwise.

## The numbers

Twenty games is a small sample, and the 10-point gap falls well within normal randomness.

- **A 45% team goes 11–9 or better about 25% of the time.** If the team were exactly as good as last year, you'd see a start like this roughly one season in four.
- **The uncertainty around 55% is wide.** A 95% confidence interval for an 11–9 record runs from about **34% to 74%**. The data fits a team that's worse than last year just as well as one that's much better.
- **A direct comparison of the two records (37/82 vs. 11/20)** gives a difference of 10 points with a standard error of about 12 points. That's a p-value around 0.4, nowhere near conventional significance.
- **One game changes the story.** At 10–10 you'd be at 50%, and the "big jump" headline would look much weaker.

## Even a real improvement wouldn't prove it's the coach

- **Schedule:** You've already noticed the early opponents were weaker. That alone could explain a couple of extra wins.
- **Roster changes:** New players could account for any difference, in either direction.
- **Other factors:** Injuries, player development, and home/away split can all play a part.

With several changes at once and only 20 games, you can't separate the coach's effect from everything else.

## Suggested framing for the preview

Accurate options that still read positively:

- *"Through 20 games under the new coach, the team is 11–9, ahead of last season's 45% pace."*
- *"An encouraging start for the new coach, though a softer early schedule and a reshuffled roster make it too soon to draw firm conclusions."*
- *"The GM credits the new coach for the improved start."* This attributes the claim to the GM instead of stating it as fact.

If you want something more solid later, compare records against the same or similar opponents. Strength-of-schedule-adjusted metrics like point differential or net rating are also more stable than win percentage. And by around 40–50 games, a gap this size starts to mean more.
